When a driver encounters an obstacle, he takes actions to stop the car.
It only takes the driver a brief moment to realize the presence of the obstacle and decide to
apply the brakes, which involves swiftly shifting his foot from the accelerator pedal to the
brake pedal.
This brief interval is commonly referred to as the reaction time. Throughout this
duration, the car continues to move at its regular and constant speed.
The distance covered by the car during this short timeframe is referred to as the
thinking distance, and it can be calculated using the equation v = d/t, where:
"d" represents the thinking distance.
"v" represents the car's speed.
"t" represents the reaction time.
As the driver applies the brakes, the car requires a certain amount of time to come to a
complete stop, during which it undergoes deceleration. In this brief interval, the car travels a
distance known as the braking distance.
Thinking and braking distance

1
Forces
You need force to start moving, but you do not
need force to keep moving with constant speed. It is
normal in physics to see a moving object with zero
force on it e.g. an object moving in space with no
friction or any object moving with constant speed.
It is normal in physics to see an object that is
moving forward while net force on it is backwards (in
opposite direction) e.g. if a car applies its brakes it is
moving forward but the resultant (net force is
backwards). Any decelerating object has force in a
direction opposite to direction of motion.

cosmic microwave background radiation
• In 1964, the US scientists Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson built a radio telescope but
struggled to eliminate noise (unwanted signal).
• It did not matter where in the sky they pointed their telescope, the noise was constant, and so
they assumed that it was a problem with their equipment.
• However, it turned out that they had accidentally discovered microwave radiation.
• Our best knowledge at the moment is that the Universe began as a hot big bang from a tiny
point smaller than a pinhead (called a singularity) about 13.8 billion years ago.
• The Universe was unimaginably hot and dense but it has been expanding and cooling ever since.
• The early Universe was so hot that neutral atoms could not form. They would instantly ionize.
• Light was continuously scattered off the charged particles (ions and electrons).
• By analogy, light is scattered in fog, which is why you cannot see very far into it.
• Once the Universe was about 379 000 years old, and about the size of the Milky Way, the
temperature dropped to 3000 K and neutral atoms formed.
• Light was no longer scattered and the Universe became transparent.
• It was like the fog suddenly lifted (disappeared) and the air became clear.
• However, the continued expansion of the Universe has caused the wavelength of this light to
redshift over time.
Hubble’s Constant:
the slope of a graph of galaxy speed against distance
Hubble’s time:
the inverse of the Hubble constant,
which gives an estimate for the age of the Universe

• Despite the name, the Big Bang was not an explosion.
• It is the expansion of the space between the galaxies.
• Imagine your universe is the two-dimensional surface of a balloon.
• Everything inside or outside of the balloon does not exist.
• As space expands (that is, the balloon inflates), clusters of galaxies move further apart with
their recession speeds increasing with distance.
• No matter the direction we look, galaxies appear to be moving away from us, suggesting we

• Supernovae occur when a large star explodes.
• The important point is that these supernovae always have the same luminosity (output power)
therefore they act as a 'standard candle'.
• By recording how bright the supernova appears to be and knowing how bright it really is, it is
possible to work out how far away it is.

### The Universe, Redshift, Hubble's Law & Orbital Speed (Unit 7: Astronomy)

Space Physics Key Equations & Concepts (Cambridge IGCSE 0625 Unit 7):
• Average orbital speed: v = 2πr / T, where r is average orbital radius and T is orbital period.
• Hubble's Law: H₀ = v / d, where v is recession speed of galaxy, d is distance, and H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹.
• Age of the Universe estimate: t = 1 / H₀ = d / v ≈ 13.8 billion years (4.5 × 10¹⁷ s).
• 1 light-year = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m (distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year).
• Redshift & Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) provide key evidence for the Big Bang theory.
